periods.activity_title: Postcards from Shaana: Entering the Text

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.118): paired sharing — a journey taken, companions, mode, learning.
Let us discuss (p.118): 'Pradesh' states — location and one special feature each.

time_bands.activity: Open by asking students where Rameswaram is and what Shaana's postcards might cover. Invite two or three quick spoken responses to warm up curiosity about India's geography.

Teacher reads the first three postcards aloud (Kashmir, Himachal, Arunachal — pp.118–122) while students follow; pause briefly at vivid details such as the four layers of clothing and the snoring that sounded like bears.
Pairs discuss the 'Let us discuss' prompt (p.118): a journey each student has enjoyed — who they went with, how they travelled, and one thing they learnt. Two or three pairs share aloud.

Whole-class activity on the 'Pradesh' states (p.118): students name as many as they can, locate each as North/East/Northeast/West/South/Centre, and recall one special feature. Teacher records responses on the board as a class-built table.

periods.teacher_notes: Shaana's opening postcards establish her chatty, observant voice — draw attention to how she mixes geography with personal detail, such as wearing four layers in Thajiwas and the treehouse walk in Arunachal. Students who are uncertain about India's regions benefit from a quick map sketch on the board before the Pradesh activity. The task on each State's facts (p.118, writing details about one's own State) is suitable for self-study at home.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Postcards: East, West, and South

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.125): complete the places-and-descriptions table from Shaana's postcards.
Let us think and reflect (p.126): Extract 1 — Sundarbans postcard, four questions on feeling and inference.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Sundarbans, Gujarat, Narmada, Goa, Chennai, and Olaikaadu postcards aloud (pp.122–125) while students follow; students note one detail from each region on a slip of paper.

Students complete the places-and-descriptions table (p.125) in pairs, drawing on the postcards just read. Teacher circulates and prompts with questions such as 'What did Shaana do at the Narmada?' before a brief whole-class share.

Class works through the four questions on Extract 1 — the Sundarbans postcard (p.126) — as a guided discussion: the MCQ on Shaana's feeling of wonder, the fill-in on why Amma is sad, the evidence for Shaana's slight nervousness, and the assertion–reason item on missing her friends. Students respond orally; teacher consolidates answers on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The Sundarbans postcard weaves two threads — ecological wonder and climate anxiety — through Shaana's humorous aside about crocodiles following her home; help students see the tonal shift from joke to Amma's sadness. The evidence for 'slight nervousness' is the line about hoping the crocodiles and snake won't follow her home — guide students to read tone as well as content. The 'Pradesh' table task (p.118, written details about one's own State/UT) remains available as self-study for students who have not yet completed it.

periods.activity_title: Tunnels, Plateaus, and Shaana's Growing Confidence

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.126–127): Extract 2 — Goa night-train postcard, four inference questions.
Let us think and reflect (p.127): questions II — Shaana's fear of tunnels, Appa/Amma's enjoyment, climate observations.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.127): extended questions — author's purpose in using postcard form, and Shaana's language of excitement and curiosity.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 2 — the Goa night-train postcard (pp.126–127) — aloud, then students work individually on the four questions: why Shaana stays awake, what she means by 'you won't believe how nice the plateaus look', her changed attitude to tunnels, and the fill-in on her wish to share the experience. Pairs compare answers briefly.

Guided discussion of questions II (p.127): the class explores why Shaana might have feared tunnels, and then finds textual evidence that Appa and Amma enjoyed themselves like children — citing moments such as Appa's snowball throwing and their diving at Olaikaadu. Teacher records strong evidence phrases on the board.

Class focuses on the two climate-change observations in the postcards — less snow in the glaciers (Kashmir) and more flooding in the Sundarbans — and discusses what these indicate about environmental change. The question on India's geographical diversity is addressed through a quick oral round-up of all regions Shaana visited.

periods.teacher_notes: Shaana's shift from fear of tunnels to wishing friends could see the plateaus is a small but telling character arc — ask students what changed for her during the journey and how her language signals that change. The climate questions (reduced snowpack, increased flooding) are deliberately child-friendly in the text; help students name the broader phenomenon without over-explaining. The two extended questions on Shaana's language of excitement and the author's purpose in using postcards (p.127) are assigned as homework; these require students to re-read the whole text independently.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Agartala, Speaking About Travel Preferences

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.131): five MCQs — meaning of Agartala, agarwood names, smell, formation, uses.
Let us speak (p.132–133): paired preference exchange using the seven travel questions and given sentence starters.

time_bands.activity: Brief orientation: tell students they will hear a short talk about a city whose name carries a hidden meaning. Ask if anyone knows where Tripura is and what Agartala might mean.

Teacher reads the Agartala transcript aloud at a measured pace (p.138 transcript). Students listen and choose the correct option for each of the five questions on p.131 — meaning of Agartala, another name for agarwood, its smell, how it forms, and its uses. Answers are discussed and confirmed whole-class.

Pairs work through the seven travel-preference questions (p.132–133) using the given sentence starters (I prefer… to… because…; I would rather… than… because…, and so on). Each student shares at least one preference with a reason; the teacher circulates and prompts students to use a different sentence starter from the list for each response.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly confuse 'beside' and 'under' when recalling place-name etymology; keep the transcript close and confirm 'tala means underneath' explicitly after the listening task. In the speaking activity, quieter students may default to very short answers — encourage them to complete at least one full sentence starter, modelling the structure on the board if needed. The agarwood transcript also carries a conservation message (the tree was nearly extinct but is now found in most homes in northern Tripura) — worth a brief mention to connect to the environmental awareness theme running through Shaana's postcards.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.133): formal leave application to the Principal — format, duration, reason, school-work plan.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the application format on the board (address, date, To The Principal, Subject, salutation, body, closing) and walks through each part, explaining its purpose and register. Students identify which parts are fixed and which require their own content.

Modelled writing: the teacher drafts the subject line and opening sentence aloud, thinking through word choices — formal vs informal — while students suggest phrasing. Verbal cues from p.133 are noted on the board.

Students write their own application independently, imagining they need leave for a family event. They must include the duration of absence, the reason, and a plan for completing missed schoolwork. Teacher circulates and gives brief individual feedback on format and register.

Two volunteers read their completed applications aloud. Class gives quick feedback — 'Is the subject line clear?', 'Is the reason formally stated?' — before the teacher summarises one or two common points about formal register.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently write the reason in informal language (e.g., 'I want to go to my cousin's wedding') — draw attention to how the model application on p.133 frames the same idea more formally. The application should be fully drafted, peer-reviewed, and revised within this sitting. Connecting to Shaana's travels (she too would have needed leave from school before her long journey) can help students see the functional relevance of the task.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.129): match six words (blink, scary, existed, amazing, splashed, floating) to context situations.
Let us learn (p.130): underline subject and verb in three sentences from the text; discuss agreement rules.
Let us learn (p.131): ten fill-in items — choose correct verb form for subject-verb agreement rules.

time_bands.activity: Students match the six context-clue situations to the words from the box (p.129): blink, scary, existed, amazing, splashed, floating. Pairs compare, then the class confirms answers — drawing each word back to its appearance in Shaana's postcards.

Teacher introduces subject-verb agreement using the three sentences from the text (p.130): 'Amma and Appa are fast asleep'; 'It's hot, dry, and there is sand everywhere'; 'There are so many hills here.' Students underline the subject and verb in each, and the teacher draws out the rules — compound subjects with 'and', existential 'there', and pronoun 'it'.

Students complete all ten fill-in items on p.131 individually, applying the rules for pairs ('a pair of'), or/nor constructions, collective nouns, and nouns plural in form but singular in meaning. Answers are shared round the class and each rule is named when confirmed.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in this set is with 'either/or' and 'neither/nor' constructions — the verb agrees with the subject closer to it; reinforce this pattern explicitly when reviewing items 2, 4, 9, and 10. The word-matching task (p.129) works best when students are asked to read the word in a postcard sentence before matching to the situation, so they see contextual meaning rather than guessing. The picture-matching task (p.128 — matching geography terms to images) and the word-grid task (p.129) are suitable self-study activities for students who finish early.

periods.activity_title: India's Landmarks: Crossword and Local Heritage Research

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.134): landmark crossword — identify States and UTs from across-and-down clues.
Let us explore (p.135): research and share unique places in your own village, region, or state.

time_bands.activity: Quick orientation: teacher shows one example clue from the crossword (Pangong Lake → Ladakh) on the board to model how landmark clues map to States/UTs. Students open the crossword on p.134.

Students work in pairs to solve as many across-and-down clues as they can in the landmark crossword (p.134). Teacher circulates and prompts with additional geographical hints where pairs are stuck — e.g., 'Gangotri Glacier is in which Himalayan state?'

Each pair then takes two minutes to recall and note what unique natural, historical, or cultural site exists in their own village, region, or state (p.135, inspired by the Ellora and Rani-ki-Vav examples). Pairs share their findings with the class; the teacher builds a quick board list of places mentioned — connecting them back to Shaana's spirit of discovery.

periods.teacher_notes: The crossword clues span the whole country — if students struggle with a particular region, prompt with the geographical zone (e.g., 'Hampi is in the Deccan') rather than revealing the answer. The local-heritage sharing works best when the teacher participates by naming one place from their own region, modelling the register of describing a place's significance. The Hornbill Festival group-research task (p.135) requires library or internet access that may not be available in this sitting and is well-suited to a self-study assignment.
materials: Atlas or outline map of India (optional)

periods.activity_title: Hornbill Festival: Group Research and Presentation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.135): groups of four research and present the Hornbill Festival — when, who, purpose, events.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly locates Nagaland on the board map, names Kohima as its capital, and introduces Kisama village as the site of the Hornbill Festival, framing it as one of India's most vivid cultural celebrations.

Groups of four use available reference material (textbooks, class library, teacher-provided notes) to find and note details about the Hornbill Festival: when it is held, which communities participate, its purpose, and the events staged. Each group assigns one member to note-take and one to lead the presentation.

Groups present their findings in turn — approximately two minutes per group. Classmates listen and are invited to ask one question each after each presentation. Teacher adds factual clarifications where needed.

Teacher draws a brief closing connection between the Hornbill Festival's celebration of Naga heritage and Shaana's journey — both are expressions of India's extraordinary cultural and geographical diversity. Students are invited to name one new thing they learnt about India across all of Shaana's postcards.

periods.teacher_notes: If printed or library reference material is limited, the teacher may prepare a brief fact-sheet about the Hornbill Festival in advance for groups to work from. Groups sometimes produce very similar presentations — encourage differentiation by assigning each group a different focal angle (history, events, food, craft, or purpose) before research begins. The closing reflection on Shaana's journey is intended to draw the chapter's themes of curiosity, diversity, and discovery together through the students' own voices.
materials: Class library / teacher fact-sheet on Hornbill Festival

items.item_stem: Read the statement below and choose the option that best describes Shaana's attitude when she writes about the Sundarbans in her postcard. 'Amma tells me that places like the Sundarbans are called wetlands. I never knew such a place existed.'

options.label: A
options.text: She is bored because she expected something more exciting.

options.label: B
options.text: She is delighted by a discovery she had not imagined before.

options.label: C
options.text: She is relieved that the journey to the Sundarbans is over.

options.label: D
options.text: She is worried that her Amma will become sadder.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests a misreading of tone — the phrase 'I never knew' signals discovery, not disappointment.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Conflates Amma's sadness about flooding with Shaana's own reaction to seeing the wetland.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a sense of relief not supported by the postcard's language or context.

items.item_stem: In her postcard from the Goa night train, Shaana writes that she 'used to be afraid of tunnels' but is not any more, and wishes her friends could someday see the plateaus together. What does this shift in Shaana's feelings, and her wish to share the experience, reveal about how travelling has changed her? Support your answer with at least two details from her postcards across the journey.

expected_elements: Names the change from fear to confidence or curiosity about new landscapes.
Cites at least one other postcard detail showing growing boldness (e.g., learning surfing, snowball throwing).
Explains the wish to share experiences as evidence of a social, outward-looking attitude.
Uses own words rather than simply copying lines from the text.

items.item_stem: Listen to the talk about Agartala and agarwood (p.138). Then fill in the blanks with information from the talk. (1) The word 'Agartala' is made up of 'agar', a type of __________, and 'tala', meaning __________. (2) Agarwood is described as smelling like a mix of __________ and __________ scents. (3) Agarwood forms only when the tree is __________ or infected, and it produces a dark, sticky substance called __________.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. tree; underneath. 2. woody; flowery. 3. hurt; agar oil.

items.item_stem: Based on the talk about agarwood that you listened to, answer the following in two or three sentences: The speaker says that agarwood was 'once almost extinct' but is now found in nearly every home in northern Tripura. What does this tell us about what people in the region did, and why is this significant?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: People in the region took deliberate care of the agar tree, which prevented its extinction. This is significant because a rare and historically important tree — used for perfumes, incense, medicine, and Tripura's famous wood carvings — was saved through community effort and is now widely available.

items.item_stem: Shaana travels through both mountains and beaches during her journey across India. Describe to your partner which of these two types of destinations you prefer for a holiday and why. Use at least one of the sentence frames you practised (such as 'I prefer… to… because…' or 'I would rather… than… because…') and give one specific reason.

expected_elements: States a clear preference between mountains and beaches.
Uses at least one comparative sentence frame correctly.
Gives a specific, relevant reason for the preference.
Speaks in complete sentences at a pace the partner can follow.

items.item_stem: Shaana's journey took her to very different regions of India — snowy glaciers, dense forests, wetlands, deserts, plateaus, and beaches. Imagine a classmate has never been outside your home district. In a short spoken exchange, try to persuade them that an adventurous trip across different regions of India — like Shaana's — would be more valuable than a comfortable trip to one familiar place. Give at least two reasons and respond to one objection your partner raises.

expected_elements: Offers at least two reasons drawing on Shaana's varied experiences (geography, culture, personal growth).
Responds to a partner's objection without dismissing it.
Uses a comparative frame ('appeals to me more than… because…' or similar) at least once.
Maintains a persuasive, courteous tone throughout.

items.item_stem: Shaana's final postcard in the chapter is written not to her classmates but to her Amma and Appa — a warm, personal note of gratitude for the journey. Imagine you have just returned from a school excursion to a place you found truly memorable. Write a letter to the teacher who organised the trip, expressing what you valued most about the experience and suggesting one addition or change that would make the trip even better for future students. Your letter should be in formal English, with a proper format.

expected_elements: Opens and closes in formal letter format with correct salutation.
Names a specific aspect of the trip found valuable, with a brief reason.
Frames the suggestion respectfully and constructively.
Maintains formal register throughout — avoids colloquial phrasing.

items.item_stem: Match each sentence from the travel context in Column A with the correct subject-verb agreement rule it illustrates in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A|Column B
Neither the guide nor the tourists were prepared for the sudden rain.|Compound subject joined by 'and' takes a plural verb
Amma and Appa are fast asleep in the tent.|Verb agrees with the subject nearest to it in 'neither/nor'
A pair of hiking boots is essential for the trek.|'A pair of' takes a singular verb
There are tall mangrove trees all around the boat.|Existential 'there' — verb agrees with the noun that follows

answer_key.left: Neither the guide nor the tourists were prepared for the sudden rain.
answer_key.right: Verb agrees with the subject nearest to it in 'neither/nor'

answer_key.left: Amma and Appa are fast asleep in the tent.
answer_key.right: Compound subject joined by 'and' takes a plural verb

answer_key.left: A pair of hiking boots is essential for the trek.
answer_key.right: 'A pair of' takes a singular verb

answer_key.left: There are tall mangrove trees all around the boat.
answer_key.right: Existential 'there' — verb agrees with the noun that follows

items.source_context: Subject-verb agreement: compound subjects with 'and', existential 'there', 'a pair of', or/nor, collective nouns, nouns plural in form but singular in meaning.
items.item_stem: Four sentences below describe scenes from Shaana's journey across India, but each contains a subject-verb agreement error. Rewrite each sentence correctly and name the agreement rule you applied. (1) Amma and Appa was amazed by the blue-white glaciers of Thajiwas. (2) Either the crocodile or the snakes were resting on the bank of the Sundarbans waterway. (3) The news about the reduced water levels in the Narmada were surprising. (4) A pair of binoculars were left behind on the rafting boat.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. 'Amma and Appa were amazed' — compound subject with 'and' takes a plural verb. 2. 'Either the crocodile or the snakes were resting' — verb agrees with the nearer subject ('snakes', plural). 3. 'The news… was surprising' — 'news' is plural in form but singular in meaning, takes a singular verb. 4. 'A pair of binoculars was left behind' — 'a pair of' takes a singular verb.

items.source_lo: Student researches and presents information about India's geographical and cultural heritage, connecting landmark knowledge to the themes of discovery and diversity in the text.

items.item_stem: Shaana's journey takes her to many regions of India, each known for a distinctive landmark or feature. Choose any three of the landmarks listed below and name the State or Union Territory each belongs to. Then write one sentence explaining what makes each landmark significant — geographically, historically, or culturally. Landmarks to choose from: Pangong Lake; Gangotri Glacier; Double Decker Living Root Bridge; Rann of Kutch; Chilika Lake; Hampi.

expected_elements: Correctly names the State or UT for each of the three chosen landmarks.
Gives a specific, accurate significance for each — not a generic statement.
Shows understanding that India's diversity spans geography, history, and culture.
Writes in clear, complete sentences with appropriate vocabulary.

items.source_lo: Student researches and presents information about India's geographical and cultural heritage, connecting landmark knowledge to the themes of discovery and diversity in the text.
items.source_context: India's States and UTs identified through landmarks (crossword); local heritage places; Hornbill Festival of Nagaland — purpose, participants, events.
items.item_stem: The Hornbill Festival, held annually in Kisama village near Kohima, Nagaland, celebrates the cultural heritage of the Naga people. Working in a group, research the festival and prepare a brief illustrated fact-file (one page) covering: (a) when and where the festival is held, (b) which communities participate and why, (c) at least three types of events or activities featured, and (d) what the festival's name refers to and why the hornbill is significant in Naga culture. Present your fact-file to the class and be ready to answer two questions from your audience.

expected_elements: Accurately states dates (first week of December) and location (Kisama Heritage Village, Kohima).
Names multiple Naga tribes as participants and links the festival to cultural preservation.
Describes at least three events — e.g., traditional dances, crafts, indigenous sports, food stalls.
Explains the hornbill's symbolic importance in Naga warrior and ceremonial culture.
